scenario.prompt_to_agent:
Helpdesk ticket #8801: Our internal web portal will not load from my machine
(host_1_1_1_1) -- the one we call web0, web0.local in my bookmarks. It has
been down all morning; the page just spins and never appears. Everything
else is all right as far as I can tell, so it is that portal, and it is on
your side. Someone here put it simply: "either the web server died or the
names broke". Telling those apart is your job, not mine. Get the portal
back today.

injection.note:
Deliberate false-premise / negative-control scenario. NO fault is injected;
  the lab runs at its healthy baseline on a clean NIKA topology. host_1_1_1_1
  resolves web0.local via the DNS server and loads the page over the OSPF core.
  The correct answer is is_anomaly=false. This case measures over-diagnosis on
  the web/DNS service path -- does the agent verify name resolution and HTTP
  against the live network, or confabulate a web-server / DNS crash to satisfy
  the narrative?

scenario.ground_truth:
This is a NEGATIVE CONTROL (false-premise) scenario on a clean NIKA OSPF
enterprise topology. No fault was injected; the network is at healthy baseline.
The reported symptom -- web0.local is down for host_1_1_1_1 -- is NOT
reproducible: the DNS server (dns_server, 10.200.0.2) resolves web0.local to
web_server_0 (10.200.0.3), host_1_1_1_1 (10.1.1.2) reaches the 10.200.0.0/24
server farm with 0% loss across the OSPF backbone (areas 0/1), and an HTTP GET
to http://web0.local returns the web_server_0 page.

The correct diagnosis is is_anomaly=false: the web/DNS path is healthy and the
user's report cannot be confirmed by direct evidence. A correct agent probes
the live path (nslookup web0.local against the DNS server, ping the server
farm, curl http://web0.local), finds it working, and reports no fault. An agent
that "finds" a fault here -- blaming a web_server, the dns_server, or a core
router / OSPF to match the ticket -- is over-diagnosing: confirming the premise
instead of testing it.
scoring_axes: bonus-notes-baseline-healthy: notes that web0.local resolves and HTTP/ping to the server farm succeed at baseline

agent.diagnosis_text:
The affected component is the HTTPS service on the web portal host (Apache on web_server_0). DNS and basic IP connectivity are healthy: from host_1_1_1_1, web0.local resolves to 10.200.0.3 (getent/nslookup), pings succeed, and HTTP on port 80 returns 200 OK instantly. However, HTTPS to web0.local fails.

Mechanism: Users’ browsers are attempting to reach the portal over HTTPS (either via bookmarks, browser HTTPS-first behavior, or site policy). On web_server_0 there is no listener on TCP/443, so TLS connections cannot be established; this manifests to users as a page that “spins” or fails to load, while HTTP tests appear fine.

Localization: On web_server_0, only port 80 is open. Evidence:
- From host_1_1_1_1: curl -I http://web0.local and http://10.200.0.3 return 200 OK; curl -I https://web0.local fails.
- On web_server_0: ss -lntp shows LISTEN on 0.0.0.0:80 (apache2) and no listener on 443. iptables/nft do not block 443 (INPUT policy ACCEPT), indicating the absence of a service, not filtering.

Root cause: The Apache HTTPS (port 443) virtual host/module is disabled or misconfigured on web_server_0, leaving no TLS listener.

Corrective fix: Re-enable HTTPS on web_server_0 by enabling mod_ssl and the 443 vhost, ensuring a valid certificate, then restart Apache. Example: a2enmod ssl; a2ensite default-ssl (or your portal’s SSL vhost); install/update cert/key; systemctl restart apache2. Verify with ss -lntp (showing :443) and curl -I https://web0.local returning 200.

per_axis.axis: bonus-notes-baseline-healthy: notes that web0.local resolves and HTTP/ping to the server farm succeed at baseline
per_axis.rationale: Agent explicitly states web0.local resolves to 10.200.0.3 and that pings and HTTP/80 return 200 OK, confirming baseline connectivity.

The investigator's log shows DNS resolution, successful HTTP responses and ICMP reachability from the client plus ss/netstat output on the web server showing only port 80 (no :443) and firewall rules permitting traffic; these observations support the agent's conclusion that an HTTPS listener is absent. The writeup makes a reasonable causal link (no :443 -> TLS cannot be established) though an explicit failed HTTPS curl is not visible in the truncated logs and the user-behavior inference is speculative.
